drills.q: A terraform plan shows changes to a security group's ingress rules that nobody made in the .tf files. What's your first hypothesis and how do you confirm it?
drills.a: Drift — someone modified the real resource outside Terraform (console, another pipeline, an incident action), and the refresh step in plan caught the mismatch and proposed reverting it. Confirm via cloud audit logs (e.g. CloudTrail) filtered to that resource around the relevant timeframe.

drills.q: The drift in the previous scenario turns out to be a legitimate emergency change made during an incident. What's the correct way to reconcile it, rather than just applying the plan?
drills.a: Update the .tf configuration to match the new, correct desired state, codifying the emergency change properly — applying the plan as shown would silently revert and re-break whatever the emergency change fixed.

drills.q: apply fails with a lock error. The CI job that appeared to hold the lock is confirmed dead. What do you do, and what's the risk if your confirmation is wrong?
drills.a: terraform force-unlock <lock-id> — but only after real confirmation (checking the CI system logs, not just elapsed time) that the holding process is genuinely dead. If it's actually still running, you now have two concurrent writers with no lock protection, exactly the corruption scenario locking exists to prevent.

drills.q: A 'harmless rename' refactor of a production database resource shows a plan with destroy then create for that resource. What's missing, and what do you do before ever applying?
drills.a: No moved block declaring the old and new addresses as the same resource. Add a moved block, re-run plan, and confirm it now shows no destroy/create for that resource before applying — plan output is the actual safety check, no refactor should be applied without verifying it first.

drills.q: A team wants to isolate dev, staging, and prod, which have meaningfully different instance sizes and resource counts. They propose using built-in terraform workspaces. What breaks, and what's the better pattern?
drills.a: Workspaces only isolate state, not configuration — genuine environment differences would have to be threaded through as terraform.workspace-conditional logic inside shared .tf files, unreadable past a couple of real differences. Better pattern: separate backend configs per environment (directory-per-environment or Terragrunt), each with its own variables.

drills.q: A shared module used by 6 teams has grown to 35+ variables and deep nested conditionals, and using it correctly now requires reading its source. What went wrong, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Over-abstraction — the module was designed to cover every team's hypothetical use case upfront instead of being extracted from proven, real duplication. Consider splitting it into smaller, purpose-specific modules per common use-case cluster rather than one maximally generic module.

drills.q: terraform plan now takes several minutes for even a one-line change on a large root module managing 400+ resources. Diagnose and fix, and name the tradeoff of the fix.
drills.a: Every plan refreshes all tracked resources against real provider APIs before diffing, regardless of change size. Fix: split state along logical/lifecycle boundaries (networking, data, app tier) into separate root modules/backends. Tradeoff: cross-boundary references now need terraform_remote_state or explicit output/variable passing, and changes spanning boundaries become multi-step instead of one atomic apply.

drills.q: A CI pipeline posts a plan for PR review, then on merge re-runs plan and apply fresh instead of applying the saved plan artifact. What's the risk?
drills.a: A TOCTOU gap — the freshly recomputed plan on merge can differ from what was actually reviewed if anything changed in the interim (another merge, real-world drift caught by a fresh refresh), meaning what gets applied may not be what a human actually approved. Apply the exact saved .tfplan artifact instead.
